abstract: Stomatal pores modulate gas exchange between plants and the environment and are the first layer of defense against pathogens entry. Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is a recognized component of the signalling network in guard cells that control stomatal responses. We previously showed that the mitochondrial H2S source {beta}-cyanoalanine synthase (CAS-C1) is required for flg22-induced stomatal closure. Using genetically encoded redox biosensors in Arabidopsis thaliana guard cells, we found that the mitochondrially-targeted H2S donor AP39 and the pathogen-associated molecular pattern (PAMP) flg22 both increased mitochondrial H2O2 within 5 min, while the flg22-triggered rise was attenuated in cas-c1 mutants. Dissipating the mitochondrial membrane potential ({Delta}{psi}m) with the uncoupler 2,4-dinitrophenol prevented both mitochondrial oxidation and stomatal closure. Cytochrome c (CYTc), the mobile electron carrier between complexes III and IV, proved essential for this pathway. CYTc-deficient lines showed a stomatal response similar than wild-type (wt) to ABA and light but failed to trigger stomatal closure upon exposure to different PAMPs. In these plants, neither AP39 nor flg22 induced guard cell mitochondrial hyperpolarization or an increase in cytosolic H2O2. By the dimedone-switch method, we show that CYTc is persulfidated in vivo, identifying this respiratory protein as a target of H2S-mediated posttranslational modification. At the whole-plant level, cytc plants were more susceptible to spray inoculation with Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato hrcC- at early stages of infection. Together, these results position CYTc as a mitochondrial node that links H2S signalling to guard cell redox dynamics during stomatal immunity.
